question: Which chapter? (greeting) Greeting: an apostle not from men
answer: Chapter 1. Paul, an apostle sent not by men but by Jesus Christ and God the Father, greets the churches of Galatia: Christ gave himself to deliver us from the present evil age.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (greeting) Greeting: an apostle not from men
answer: Personal defense (1-2), chapter 1. Paul, an apostle sent not by men but by Jesus Christ and God the Father, greets the churches of Galatia: Christ gave himself to deliver us from the present evil age.

question: Which chapter? (argument) No other gospel
answer: Chapter 1. Paul is astonished the Galatians are deserting to a different gospel and says anyone, even an angel from heaven, who preaches a contrary gospel should be accursed.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (argument) No other gospel
answer: Personal defense (1-2), chapter 1. Paul is astonished the Galatians are deserting to a different gospel and says anyone, even an angel from heaven, who preaches a contrary gospel should be accursed.

question: Which chapter? (narrative) A gospel received by revelation
answer: Chapter 1. Paul's gospel is not man's gospel: he did not receive it from any man but through a revelation of Jesus Christ.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (narrative) A gospel received by revelation
answer: Personal defense (1-2), chapter 1. Paul's gospel is not man's gospel: he did not receive it from any man but through a revelation of Jesus Christ.

question: Which chapter? (narrative) Paul's former life in Judaism
answer: Chapter 1. Paul violently persecuted the church of God and advanced in Judaism, extremely zealous for the traditions of his fathers.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (narrative) Paul's former life in Judaism
answer: Personal defense (1-2), chapter 1. Paul violently persecuted the church of God and advanced in Judaism, extremely zealous for the traditions of his fathers.

question: Which chapter? (narrative) Called by grace; off to Arabia and Damascus
answer: Chapter 1. God, who set Paul apart before he was born, revealed his Son to him to preach among the Gentiles; Paul consulted no one but went away into Arabia and returned to Damascus.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (narrative) Called by grace; off to Arabia and Damascus
answer: Personal defense (1-2), chapter 1. God, who set Paul apart before he was born, revealed his Son to him to preach among the Gentiles; Paul consulted no one but went away into Arabia and returned to Damascus.

question: Which chapter? (narrative) First Jerusalem visit: fifteen days with Cephas
answer: Chapter 1. After three years Paul went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas for fifteen days, seeing no other apostle except James the Lord's brother.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (narrative) First Jerusalem visit: fifteen days with Cephas
answer: Personal defense (1-2), chapter 1. After three years Paul went up to Jerusalem to visit Cephas for fifteen days, seeing no other apostle except James the Lord's brother.

question: Which chapter? (narrative) In Syria and Cilicia; the Judean churches glorify God
answer: Chapter 1. Paul went to Syria and Cilicia, still unknown in person to the churches of Judea, who heard that their former persecutor now preached the faith and glorified God.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (narrative) In Syria and Cilicia; the Judean churches glorify God
answer: Personal defense (1-2), chapter 1. Paul went to Syria and Cilicia, still unknown in person to the churches of Judea, who heard that their former persecutor now preached the faith and glorified God.

question: Which chapter? (narrative) Second Jerusalem visit with Barnabas and Titus
answer: Chapter 2. After fourteen years Paul went up with Barnabas and Titus, set his gospel before the leaders privately, and refused to yield to false brothers; Titus, a Greek, was not forced to be circumcised.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (narrative) Second Jerusalem visit with Barnabas and Titus
answer: Personal defense (1-2), chapter 2. After fourteen years Paul went up with Barnabas and Titus, set his gospel before the leaders privately, and refused to yield to false brothers; Titus, a Greek, was not forced to be circumcised.

question: Which chapter? (narrative) The pillars give the right hand of fellowship
answer: Chapter 2. James, Cephas and John, the 'pillars', recognized that Paul was entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised and gave him and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, asking only that they remember the poor.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (narrative) The pillars give the right hand of fellowship
answer: Personal defense (1-2), chapter 2. James, Cephas and John, the 'pillars', recognized that Paul was entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised and gave him and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, asking only that they remember the poor.

question: Which chapter? (narrative) Paul opposes Cephas at Antioch
answer: Chapter 2. When Cephas withdrew from eating with Gentiles for fear of the circumcision party, and even Barnabas was led astray, Paul opposed him to his face before them all.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (narrative) Paul opposes Cephas at Antioch
answer: Personal defense (1-2), chapter 2. When Cephas withdrew from eating with Gentiles for fear of the circumcision party, and even Barnabas was led astray, Paul opposed him to his face before them all.

question: Which chapter? (argument) Justified by faith, not by works of the law
answer: Chapter 2. Even Jews by birth know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (argument) Justified by faith, not by works of the law
answer: Personal defense (1-2), chapter 2. Even Jews by birth know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.

question: Which chapter? (argument) Crucified with Christ
answer: Chapter 2. Through the law Paul died to the law; he has been crucified with Christ and now lives by faith in the Son of God, for if righteousness came through the law, Christ died for no purpose.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (argument) Crucified with Christ
answer: Personal defense (1-2), chapter 2. Through the law Paul died to the law; he has been crucified with Christ and now lives by faith in the Son of God, for if righteousness came through the law, Christ died for no purpose.

question: Which chapter? (argument) O foolish Galatians: the Spirit by hearing with faith
answer: Chapter 3. Paul asks whether they received the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith, and whether, having begun by the Spirit, they are now being perfected by the flesh.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (argument) O foolish Galatians: the Spirit by hearing with faith
answer: Doctrinal argument (3-4), chapter 3. Paul asks whether they received the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith, and whether, having begun by the Spirit, they are now being perfected by the flesh.

question: Which chapter? (illustration) Abraham believed God
answer: Chapter 3. Abraham believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness, so those of faith are sons of Abraham, and in him all the nations are blessed.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (illustration) Abraham believed God
answer: Doctrinal argument (3-4), chapter 3. Abraham believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness, so those of faith are sons of Abraham, and in him all the nations are blessed.

question: Which chapter? (argument) Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law
answer: Chapter 3. All who rely on works of the law are under a curse, but Christ became a curse for us ('hanged on a tree') so the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (argument) Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law
answer: Doctrinal argument (3-4), chapter 3. All who rely on works of the law are under a curse, but Christ became a curse for us ('hanged on a tree') so the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles.

question: Which chapter? (illustration) The covenant and Abraham's offspring
answer: Chapter 3. Like a ratified human covenant, God's promise to Abraham and his offspring (singular, Christ) cannot be annulled by the law that came 430 years later.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (illustration) The covenant and Abraham's offspring
answer: Doctrinal argument (3-4), chapter 3. Like a ratified human covenant, God's promise to Abraham and his offspring (singular, Christ) cannot be annulled by the law that came 430 years later.

question: Which chapter? (argument) Why then the law?
answer: Chapter 3. The law was added because of transgressions until the offspring should come, put in place through angels by an intermediary, and the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (argument) Why then the law?
answer: Doctrinal argument (3-4), chapter 3. The law was added because of transgressions until the offspring should come, put in place through angels by an intermediary, and the Scripture imprisoned everything under sin.

question: Which chapter? (illustration) The law was our guardian
answer: Chapter 3. Before faith came we were held captive under the law as under a guardian until Christ came; now that faith has come we are no longer under a guardian.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (illustration) The law was our guardian
answer: Doctrinal argument (3-4), chapter 3. Before faith came we were held captive under the law as under a guardian until Christ came; now that faith has come we are no longer under a guardian.

question: Which chapter? (argument) All one in Christ Jesus
answer: Chapter 3. All who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ: there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male and female, and all are Abraham's offspring and heirs.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (argument) All one in Christ Jesus
answer: Doctrinal argument (3-4), chapter 3. All who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ: there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male and female, and all are Abraham's offspring and heirs.

question: Which chapter? (illustration) The heir who is still a child
answer: Chapter 4. An underage heir is no different from a slave, but in the fullness of time God sent his Son so we might receive adoption as sons and cry 'Abba! Father!'

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (illustration) The heir who is still a child
answer: Doctrinal argument (3-4), chapter 4. An underage heir is no different from a slave, but in the fullness of time God sent his Son so we might receive adoption as sons and cry 'Abba! Father!'

question: Which chapter? (argument) Turning back to weak elementary principles
answer: Chapter 4. Having come to know God, how can the Galatians turn back to the weak and worthless elementary principles, observing days, months, seasons and years?

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (argument) Turning back to weak elementary principles
answer: Doctrinal argument (3-4), chapter 4. Having come to know God, how can the Galatians turn back to the weak and worthless elementary principles, observing days, months, seasons and years?

question: Which chapter? (narrative) Paul's illness and the Galatians' first welcome
answer: Chapter 4. Paul first preached to them because of a bodily ailment, and they received him as an angel of God and would have given him their eyes; has he now become their enemy by telling the truth?

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (narrative) Paul's illness and the Galatians' first welcome
answer: Doctrinal argument (3-4), chapter 4. Paul first preached to them because of a bodily ailment, and they received him as an angel of God and would have given him their eyes; has he now become their enemy by telling the truth?

question: Which chapter? (exhortation) Until Christ is formed in you
answer: Chapter 4. The agitators court the Galatians for no good purpose, while Paul is again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in his little children.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (exhortation) Until Christ is formed in you
answer: Doctrinal argument (3-4), chapter 4. The agitators court the Galatians for no good purpose, while Paul is again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in his little children.

question: Which chapter? (illustration) Hagar and Sarah: two covenants
answer: Chapter 4. Abraham's two sons, by a slave woman and a free woman, picture two covenants: Hagar is Mount Sinai and the present Jerusalem in slavery, but the Jerusalem above is free and is our mother.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (illustration) Hagar and Sarah: two covenants
answer: Doctrinal argument (3-4), chapter 4. Abraham's two sons, by a slave woman and a free woman, picture two covenants: Hagar is Mount Sinai and the present Jerusalem in slavery, but the Jerusalem above is free and is our mother.

question: Which chapter? (illustration) Children of the free woman
answer: Chapter 4. Like Isaac, believers are children of promise; Scripture says to cast out the slave woman and her son, for we are children of the free woman.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (illustration) Children of the free woman
answer: Doctrinal argument (3-4), chapter 4. Like Isaac, believers are children of promise; Scripture says to cast out the slave woman and her son, for we are children of the free woman.

question: Which chapter? (exhortation) Stand firm in freedom
answer: Chapter 5. Christ has set us free, so do not submit again to a yoke of slavery: accepting circumcision obligates one to the whole law, but in Christ only faith working through love counts.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (exhortation) Stand firm in freedom
answer: Practical living (5-6), chapter 5. Christ has set us free, so do not submit again to a yoke of slavery: accepting circumcision obligates one to the whole law, but in Christ only faith working through love counts.

question: Which chapter? (exhortation) A little leaven
answer: Chapter 5. The Galatians were running well until someone hindered them; a little leaven leavens the whole lump, and Paul wishes those who unsettle them would emasculate themselves.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (exhortation) A little leaven
answer: Practical living (5-6), chapter 5. The Galatians were running well until someone hindered them; a little leaven leavens the whole lump, and Paul wishes those who unsettle them would emasculate themselves.

question: Which chapter? (exhortation) Called to freedom: serve one another
answer: Chapter 5. Do not use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh but through love serve one another, for the whole law is fulfilled in 'love your neighbor as yourself.'

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (exhortation) Called to freedom: serve one another
answer: Practical living (5-6), chapter 5. Do not use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh but through love serve one another, for the whole law is fulfilled in 'love your neighbor as yourself.'

question: Which chapter? (exhortation) Walk by the Spirit
answer: Chapter 5. Walk by the Spirit and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh, for the flesh and the Spirit are opposed to each other.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (exhortation) Walk by the Spirit
answer: Practical living (5-6), chapter 5. Walk by the Spirit and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh, for the flesh and the Spirit are opposed to each other.

question: Which chapter? (exhortation) The works of the flesh
answer: Chapter 5. The works of the flesh, from sexual immorality and idolatry to envy and drunkenness, are evident, and those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (exhortation) The works of the flesh
answer: Practical living (5-6), chapter 5. The works of the flesh, from sexual immorality and idolatry to envy and drunkenness, are evident, and those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.

question: Which chapter? (exhortation) The fruit of the Spirit
answer: Chapter 5. The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control; those who belong to Christ keep in step with the Spirit.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (exhortation) The fruit of the Spirit
answer: Practical living (5-6), chapter 5. The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control; those who belong to Christ keep in step with the Spirit.

question: Which chapter? (exhortation) Bear one another's burdens
answer: Chapter 6. Restore a brother caught in transgression in a spirit of gentleness, bear one another's burdens to fulfill the law of Christ, and let each test his own work.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (exhortation) Bear one another's burdens
answer: Practical living (5-6), chapter 6. Restore a brother caught in transgression in a spirit of gentleness, bear one another's burdens to fulfill the law of Christ, and let each test his own work.

question: Which chapter? (exhortation) Sowing and reaping
answer: Chapter 6. God is not mocked: whatever one sows he will reap, so let us not grow weary of doing good, especially to the household of faith.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (exhortation) Sowing and reaping
answer: Practical living (5-6), chapter 6. God is not mocked: whatever one sows he will reap, so let us not grow weary of doing good, especially to the household of faith.

question: Which chapter? (argument) Large letters: boast only in the cross
answer: Chapter 6. Writing in large letters with his own hand, Paul says the circumcision party wants to boast in their flesh, but he boasts only in the cross, for what counts is a new creation.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (argument) Large letters: boast only in the cross
answer: Practical living (5-6), chapter 6. Writing in large letters with his own hand, Paul says the circumcision party wants to boast in their flesh, but he boasts only in the cross, for what counts is a new creation.

question: Which chapter? (closing) Final greeting: the marks of Jesus
answer: Chapter 6. Paul bears on his body the marks of Jesus and closes: the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers.

question: Which section: Personal defense (1-2) or Doctrinal argument (3-4) or Practical living (5-6)? (closing) Final greeting: the marks of Jesus
answer: Practical living (5-6), chapter 6. Paul bears on his body the marks of Jesus and closes: the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers.

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “Paul, an apostle—not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead”
answer: The opening words of the letter, stressing that his apostleship came directly from Christ and God, not from any human authority. (Chapter 1)

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel”
answer: Skipping his usual thanksgiving, Paul goes straight to rebuking the Galatians for turning to another gospel. (Chapter 1)

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed.”
answer: Warning the Galatians against the different gospel being taught by those troubling them; he repeats the curse in the next verse. (Chapter 1)

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ.”
answer: Defending himself against the charge that he softened the gospel to win human approval. (Chapter 1)

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ.”
answer: Explaining the source of his gospel before recounting his life story. (Chapter 1)

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “how I persecuted the church of God violently and tried to destroy it”
answer: Recalling his former life in Judaism, before God called him. (Chapter 1)

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “In what I am writing to you, before God, I do not lie!”
answer: An oath in the middle of describing his first Jerusalem visit, when he saw only Cephas and James. (Chapter 1)

question: Who said: “He who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.”
answer: The churches of Judea (what they kept hearing about Paul). While Paul was in Syria and Cilicia, still unknown in person to the Judean churches; they glorified God because of him.

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “to them we did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved for you”
answer: About the false brothers who slipped in to spy out their freedom during his second Jerusalem visit, when Titus was not forced to be circumcised. (Chapter 2)

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “what they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality”
answer: An aside about the leaders in Jerusalem who "seemed to be influential"; they added nothing to his gospel. (Chapter 2)

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “Only, they asked us to remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.”
answer: The one request James, Cephas and John made when they gave Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship. (Chapter 2)

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned.”
answer: Introducing the incident at Antioch where Peter (Cephas) withdrew from eating with Gentile believers. (Chapter 2)

question: Who said: “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews?”
answer: Paul, to Cephas (Peter) "before them all". At Antioch, after Peter drew back from eating with the Gentiles when men came from James, and even Barnabas was led astray. (Peter himself has no recorded words in Galatians.)

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ”
answer: Continuing from his rebuke of Peter at Antioch: even Jews by birth know this. (Chapter 2)

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me.”
answer: Explaining that through the law he died to the law so that he might live to God. (Chapter 2)

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “for if righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose”
answer: The conclusion of his argument after the Antioch episode: he does not nullify the grace of God. (Chapter 2)

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you?”
answer: Opening his doctrinal argument: Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified before their eyes. (Chapter 3)

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh?”
answer: Asking whether they received the Spirit by works of the law or by hearing with faith. (Chapter 3)

question: Which Old Testament passage is Paul quoting? “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”
answer: Genesis 15:6. Paul cites Abraham as proof that righteousness comes by faith: those of faith are the sons of Abraham.

question: Who said: “In you shall all the nations be blessed.”
answer: God, speaking to Abraham (the Scripture "preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham"). Paul says the Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith.

question: Which Old Testament passage is Paul quoting? “In you shall all the nations be blessed.”
answer: Genesis 12:3. Paul says the Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith.

question: Who said: “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.”
answer: Moses, in the curses of the Law. Paul argues that all who rely on works of the law are under a curse.

question: Which Old Testament passage is Paul quoting? “Cursed be everyone who does not abide by all things written in the Book of the Law, and do them.”
answer: Deuteronomy 27:26. Paul argues that all who rely on works of the law are under a curse.

question: Who said: “The righteous shall live by faith.”
answer: God, answering the prophet Habakkuk. Paul shows that no one is justified before God by the law.

question: Which Old Testament passage is Paul quoting? “The righteous shall live by faith.”
answer: Habakkuk 2:4. Paul shows that no one is justified before God by the law.

question: Who said: “The one who does them shall live by them.”
answer: God, giving the law through Moses. Paul contrasts the law with faith: the law is not of faith.

question: Which Old Testament passage is Paul quoting? “The one who does them shall live by them.”
answer: Leviticus 18:5. Paul contrasts the law with faith: the law is not of faith.

question: Who said: “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”
answer: Moses, in the Law. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.

question: Which Old Testament passage is Paul quoting? “Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree”
answer: Deuteronomy 21:23. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.

question: Who said: “And to your offspring”
answer: God, promising to Abraham. Paul notes the promise says "offspring," not "offsprings," referring to one: Christ.

question: Which Old Testament passage is Paul quoting? “And to your offspring”
answer: Genesis 12:7 (also 13:15; 22:18). Paul notes the promise says "offspring," not "offsprings," referring to one: Christ.

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “the law, which came 430 years afterward, does not annul a covenant previously ratified by God”
answer: Using the human example of a ratified covenant to show that the law cannot cancel the promise to Abraham. (Chapter 3)

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “Why then the law? It was added because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made”
answer: Answering the obvious objection after arguing that the inheritance comes by promise, not by law. (Chapter 3)

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “So then, the law was our guardian until Christ came, in order that we might be justified by faith.”
answer: Describing the law as a temporary guardian; now that faith has come we are no longer under it. (Chapter 3)

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.”
answer: All who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ and are sons of God through faith. (Chapter 3)

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law”
answer: Following the illustration of the heir who is still a child, under guardians until the date set by his father. (Chapter 4)

question: Who said: “Abba! Father!”
answer: The Spirit of God's Son, crying in our hearts. Because believers are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts.

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “You observe days and months and seasons and years!”
answer: Rebuking the Galatians for turning back to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world. (Chapter 4)

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “if possible, you would have gouged out your eyes and given them to me”
answer: Remembering how warmly they welcomed him when he first preached to them because of a bodily ailment. (Chapter 4)

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth?”
answer: Contrasting their first welcome with their present attitude toward him. (Chapter 4)

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “my little children, for whom I am again in the anguish of childbirth until Christ is formed in you!”
answer: A tender personal appeal; he is perplexed about them and wishes he could be present. (Chapter 4)

question: Who said: “Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor!”
answer: The prophet Isaiah. Paul applies it to the free "Jerusalem above," our mother, in his allegory of Hagar and Sarah.

question: Which Old Testament passage is Paul quoting? “Rejoice, O barren one who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who are not in labor!”
answer: Isaiah 54:1. Paul applies it to the free "Jerusalem above," our mother, in his allegory of Hagar and Sarah.

question: Who said: “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with the son of the free woman.”
answer: Sarah, demanding that Abraham send away Hagar and Ishmael. Paul quotes it as "the Scripture" to conclude the Hagar and Sarah allegory: we are children of the free woman.

question: Which Old Testament passage is Paul quoting? “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not inherit with the son of the free woman.”

question: Which Old Testament passage is Paul quoting? “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
answer: Leviticus 19:18. Paul says the whole law is fulfilled in this one word, so use freedom to serve one another through love.

question: What was the context? Paul wrote: “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh.”
